About: spontaneous symmetry breaking in the 2D Ising ferromagnet

Source

Concept
2D square-lattice Ising model, exact Metropolis dynamics (J = kB = 1, periodic L×L lattice). Whether — and at what temperature — order appears is exactly what the inquiry has you measure for yourself.
Serves
Statistical mechanics / phase transitions: order parameter, critical temperature, critical fluctuations and slowing down, finite-size effects.
Inquiry
Predict the outcome of slow cooling, then the behaviour of the signed trace near Tc; measure ⟨|M|⟩ yourself and place your own Tc guess before the exact curve is shown.
Misconception
"Order needs an organiser — something must favour up." Does it? The inquiry's prediction cards put exactly that to the test — cool the grid and watch. (The outcome fills in here once the inquiry is complete.)

Pedagogy principles applied

Predict before revealTwo gated prediction cards; each distractor is a real student intuition (order needs a field, symmetry forces a 50/50 split, "up" is preferred).
Invariant made visibleThe rule's up/down symmetry never changes; only the run's outcome does — the signed trace records the choice run after run.
Operational numbersEvery displayed number is measured from the live lattice or computed from the exact kernel formulas, with units in J/kB.
Honest dataThe finite-grid tail above Tc is shown, never subtracted; the exact infinite-lattice curve is labelled and sits below the hot-side dots.
Felt physicsThe record ring counts sweeps, and near the transition a measurement deliberately takes ×3 the sweeps — successive sweeps decorrelate slowly there, so the honest price of a clean average is felt as a longer wait.
Formal layer optionalMetropolis rule, Onsager Tc, M(T) and the finite-size shift live behind ⚛︎ The Physics, the pop-up revision sheet.

Guided Inquiry

1 · A hot grid of stubborn neighbours

Each spin gains only by matching its four neighbours — nothing in the rule prefers up or down. The grid starts hot at T = 3.0 J/kB. Press ▶ Play and watch the mess shimmer.

2 · Predict: what does slow cooling make?

Suppose you now cool slowly to T = 1.6 J/kB and wait. What does the settled grid look like?

3 · Cool it and watch

Drag T slowly down toward 1.6 J/kB. Patches of both colours grow, merge and fight. Watch the signed M trace as one colour takes the frame.

4 · Symmetry in the rule, choice in the run

Order appeared with no organiser. Drag T back up to 3.0 — let the grid scramble to fresh noise — then cool once more. The trace's sign records which way this run chose.

5 · Predict: the trace at T = 2.30

Suppose you park T at 2.30 J/kB and leave it there. What does the signed M trace do?

6 · Where deciding is slow

Set T ≈ 2.30 and watch the trace wander. Then press ⏺ Record: successive sweeps decorrelate so slowly here that the measurement takes ×3 the sweeps — the ring shows that price.

7 · Measure, map, then reveal

Record ⟨|M|⟩ at least six temperatures, spanning clearly-ordered and clearly-mixed. Drag the flag to where the rise begins — the exact curve appears only once your map is in. Then rerun at L = 32: does the rise move? Which way?

8 · Why a toy carries real physics

Magnets, liquid–vapour, alloys: all order this way near their critical points, with the same exponents. A liquid near its critical point shows the same slow, large swings — what plays the role of M there?

The Physics

The 2D Ising model · a complete revision sheet · spontaneous magnetisation and the order–disorder transition

Spontaneous magnetisation isn't an order obeyed. It's a rule with no preference discovering that below one temperature, agreeing everywhere costs less than not — and the direction is this run's accident.

01

Nothing favours up. So where does the order come from?

Three moments from one continuously-cooled run of the sim's own Metropolis kernel on its 32×32 periodic lattice — same rule, same colours the sim paints.
  • The whole model is one line: a neighbouring pair costs −J when the two spins match, +J when they don't. There is no field term, so up and down are exactly interchangeable.
  • Energy alone would freeze the grid into one colour; temperature alone would scramble it. Every configuration is weighed by both — that competition is the whole story.
  • Hot, the winner changes every few spins and the signed M shimmers near zero. Cold, a purely local preference for matching ends up ordering the whole grid.
  • Between them sits one temperature where patches of every size coexist. That is the transition, and the middle panel is what it looks like.
The energy the sim's flip rule implements, with J = kB = 1 and no external field.
02

What actually decides a single flip?

The sim's Metropolis rule, exactly as its code computes it — ΔE takes only five values.
One attempted flip, and the acceptance probabilities the sim's own acceptProb returns at two temperatures.
  • Pick a site at random, compute ΔE = 2J si Σ sj over its four neighbours. On a square lattice that can only be −8, −4, 0, +4 or +8 J.
  • Downhill or flat is taken every time — probability exactly 1. Uphill is taken with probability e−ΔE/kBT: for +4J that is 0.082 at T = 1.6 and 0.264 at T = 3.0. Heat is what buys disagreement.
  • One sweep is L² such attempts. Sweeps are Monte-Carlo time, not seconds — the sweeps-per-second slider only sets how fast you watch.
  • min(1, e−ΔE/kBT) satisfies detailed balance, so the run samples the canonical ensemble at T: fixed, distinguishable lattice sites, zero field, and total magnetisation not conserved.
03

How much order, and below exactly what temperature?

Onsager's exact critical point — the self-dual condition sinh(2J/kBTc) = 1.
Exact spontaneous magnetisation (Onsager–Yang). The exponent is β = 1/8 exactly — not mean-field's 1/2, and not a fit.
T L

These are the sim's real Temperature slider and Grid size selector — drag here and the lattice follows.

The sim's own measurement panel, reproduced: the exact curve it reveals, its Tc and apparent-Tc lines, and 15 dots recorded the way its ⏺ Record button records them.
The finite-size shift the sim quotes: ν = 1 is exact in 2D, a ≈ 0.8 is an empirical amplitude — so an L×L grid finds the transition warm by about Tc·0.8/L.
  • Below Tc the exact curve rises as B(1 − T/Tc)1/8 with B ≈ 1.22. An eighth root is brutally steep: 1% below Tc the order parameter is already 0.686, and 0.1% below it is still 0.515. That is why the rise looks like a cliff.
  • The dots track the exact curve to about 0.003 once T ≤ 2.0, then scatter badly from Tc up to about 2.4 — and that scatter is the physics, not sloppiness.
  • Measurement hygiene. Record sweeps the live lattice, so it inherits whatever state you left it in. Quench straight from hot to cold and you can freeze in a pair of domain walls wrapping the torus — the sim calls that trapped stripes. Reheat and cool gradually.
04

If the rule is symmetric, how can one direction win?

The two numbers on screen: the trace keeps the sign, each plotted dot is a time average of the size.
  • Strictly, on a finite L×L grid at zero field the equilibrium average of the signed M is exactly zero — given long enough the grid flips wholesale and visits both ordered states.
  • "Long enough" grows exponentially with L. At L = 64 below Tc it dwarfs any session, so the trace pins. The symmetry is broken in practice here; only in the L → ∞ limit is it broken in principle.
  • That is exactly why the plot averages |M| while the trace keeps the sign: up-ordered and down-ordered are the same amount of order.
  • Press ↻ Reset and cool again. The sim draws a fresh random seed each run, so the other sign comes up about as often — nothing is loaded.
05

Why should a toy square lattice matter?

Same shape of statement, different number: the exact 2D dome this sim draws, against the 3D Ising exponent real magnets and fluids follow.
  • Near Tc the correlation length outgrows every microscopic scale, so the lattice, the bond strength and the chemistry all stop mattering. Only dimensionality and the symmetry of the order parameter survive. That is universality.
  • The order parameter changes name, not role: magnetisation in a ferromagnet, the liquid–vapour density difference ρliq − ρvap in a fluid, sublattice occupancy in a binary alloy. Each vanishes at its critical point.
  • Be exact about the number: β = 1/8 is the two-dimensional result, which is what this sim draws. Real three-dimensional magnets and fluids sit in the 3D Ising class, β ≈ 0.326 — same story, different exponent.
  • Onsager solved the 2D model in 1944; that is the only reason any of these numbers are known exactly. Above two dimensions it is renormalisation group and numerics.
06

The traps they'll set for you

  • "Order needs an organiser — something must favour up." Nothing does: the field is zero and the flip rule is symmetric. Below Tc, global agreement simply costs less than disagreement — in either direction.
  • "Then it should settle half up, half down." Two equal halves need a long wall of mismatched neighbours, and walls cost energy. The symmetry lives in the rule, not in each run's outcome.
  • "The transition on the screen is sharp, and reads zero above it." Neither. On L = 32–96 the rise is rounded and sits warm — the sim's estimate is Tc(1 + 0.8/L) ≈ 2.2976 at L = 64 — and above Tc a finite grid still shows ⟨|M|⟩ ≈ 0.04 at L = 64 (≈ 0.10 at L = 32), a tail that falls like 1/L and is shown, never subtracted.
  • "A dot near 2.3 is as trustworthy as one at 1.6." It is not. Near Tc successive sweeps stay correlated far longer, so 400 sweeps contain far fewer independent samples. That is why ⏺ Record takes ×3 as many sweeps there and why the ± spread balloons — it is a spread, not an error bar.
07

Ninety-second self-test

Drag T to the coldest the slider goes, 1.0 J/kB. Does ⟨|M|⟩ reach exactly 1?

No. Onsager gives M(1.0) = 0.9993 and the sim measures 0.999: even at T = 1.0 a handful of spins are flipped at any instant. Only T = 0 gives a perfectly aligned grid.

You switch from L = 64 to L = 32 and remeasure. Which way does the apparent Tc move, and what happens to the hot-side dots?

Warmer: Tc(1 + 0.8/L) goes from ≈ 2.2976 to ≈ 2.3259, about +0.028 J/kB. And the tail above Tc roughly doubles, because it falls as 1/L — the sim's kernel gives ≈ 0.04 at L = 64 and ≈ 0.10 at L = 32 for T = 3.0.

Why does the plot average |M| when the trace keeps the sign?

Because the two ordered states are equally likely, so the signed M averages to zero and would hide the order completely. |M| measures how much order there is regardless of which direction this run happened to choose.
